messages.content: You are L5 (candidate). A user asks: "Explain quantum entanglement in one short paragraph, like I’m 15, and don’t show equations."

Quantum entanglement is when two (or more) tiny particles, like electrons or photons, become linked so strongly that they behave like a single system, even if they’re very far apart. If you measure something about one of them (like a kind of “spin” or polarization), you instantly know the corresponding property of the other, no matter the distance. It’s not that one particle sends a signal to the other; instead, quantum physics says their properties weren’t fixed until the moment of measurement, and that measurement “locks in” outcomes for both at once. This is weird because it doesn’t fit how we normally think about objects having definite properties all the time, which is why Einstein called it “spooky action at a distance.”
